hook.text: Every commuter prefers driving. If everyone drives, traffic is gridlocked. The bus would've been faster for all.

buildup.text: A social dilemma: individual rationality produces collective irrationality. What's best for me hurts us all.

discovery.text: The structure is always the same: a dominant strategy for each player leads to a dominated outcome for the group.

twist.text: Social dilemmas aren't failures of morality—they're failures of structure. Smart people make bad outcomes inevitable.

climax.text: Climate change, overfishing, arms races, and antibiotic overuse are all social dilemmas hiding in plain sight.

punchline.text: When everyone optimizes alone, everyone loses.

quiz.question: What defines a social dilemma?
options: Individual rationality leads to collectively worse outcomes

hook.text: Four players each get $10. Anything put into a shared pool doubles and splits equally. What do you contribute?

buildup.text: If everyone gives $10, the pool becomes $80 and each gets $20. But free riders keep $10 and still get the split.

discovery.text: In experiments, contributions start at 50% and collapse near zero by round 10. Cooperation erodes without enforcement.

twist.text: Add punishment—let players pay to fine free riders—and cooperation soars to 90%. The threat of sanctions works.

climax.text: Public goods everywhere—roads, parks, national defense—face this exact dilemma. Taxes are the punishment mechanism.

punchline.text: Public goods need public enforcement.

quiz.question: What happens in public goods games without punishment?

hook.text: Someone must call 911. If nobody calls, the victim dies. But calling costs time. Everyone waits for someone else.

buildup.text: The volunteer's dilemma: someone must bear a cost so everyone benefits—but each person hopes another will volunteer.

discovery.text: The bystander effect is this dilemma in action. More witnesses mean less likelihood any individual calls for help.

twist.text: Kitty Genovese's 1964 murder became famous: reportedly 38 witnesses, nobody called police. Diffusion of responsibility.

climax.text: Solutions assign responsibility: fire drills pick specific people. 'You in the red shirt, call 911' breaks the dilemma.

punchline.text: When everyone can help, often nobody does.

quiz.question: What causes the bystander effect?

hook.text: Two cars race toward each other. The first to swerve is 'chicken.' But if neither swerves, both die.

buildup.text: The game of chicken has two equilibria: I swerve and you don't, or you swerve and I don't. But which?

discovery.text: The key: credibly committing to not swerve forces the other to back down. Throw your steering wheel out the window.

twist.text: The Cuban Missile Crisis was chicken: both sides escalated, hoping the other would blink. The world nearly ended.

climax.text: Business uses chicken too: price wars, standard battles, and market entry races all have the same terrible structure.

punchline.text: The bravest move might be to swerve first.

quiz.question: What makes the chicken game dangerous?
options: Both players holding firm leads to the worst outcome

hook.text: Two players take turns. Each round the pot grows. Grab it or pass. Passing doubles it, but risks the other grabbing.

buildup.text: Backward induction says grab round 1. In the last round, your opponent grabs. So grab the round before. And before.

discovery.text: Logic says grab immediately. But experiments show most players pass for several rounds, growing the pot cooperatively.

twist.text: Humans are 'irrationally' cooperative—and richer for it. The rational play leaves both players with almost nothing.

climax.text: The centipede game reveals how rigid rationality can destroy value. Sometimes trusting a bit longer pays off hugely.

punchline.text: Strict logic says grab now. Trust says wait.

quiz.question: What does backward induction predict in the centipede game?

hook.text: Every country benefits from cheap fossil fuels. Every country suffers from climate change. Nobody wants to cut first.

buildup.text: Climate change is the ultimate social dilemma: the atmosphere is a global commons and emission cuts are costly.

discovery.text: The Paris Agreement used voluntary pledges over binding cuts. Game theory predicted this: no country wants enforcement.

twist.text: Pledges are cheap talk. Without penalties, each nation has incentives to promise big and deliver little.

climax.text: William Nordhaus proposed a 'climate club': members set carbon tariffs on non-members. He won the 2018 Nobel Prize.

punchline.text: The planet has a free-rider problem.

quiz.question: Why is climate change a social dilemma?
options: Individual countries benefit from emitting but suffer collectively

hook.text: Atlantic cod fed millions for centuries. In 1992, the population collapsed to 1% of historic levels. The fishery closed.

buildup.text: Each fishing boat takes more because if they don't, someone else will. Individual restraint just hands fish to rivals.

discovery.text: This is a common-pool resource dilemma: the ocean is open, fish move freely, and no one owns the stock.

twist.text: Iceland solved it with transferable quotas: each boat owns a share of the total catch. Ownership creates care.

climax.text: Where quotas were adopted, fish stocks recovered. Where they weren't, collapse continued. Institutions beat intentions.

punchline.text: Own a share of the fish, and you'll protect the fish.

quiz.question: How did Iceland solve overfishing?
options: Assigned individual transferable quotas to boats

hook.text: The Nile feeds 11 countries. Ethiopia built a dam. Egypt says it threatens their water supply. Who owns a river?

buildup.text: Shared rivers are social dilemmas: upstream countries can take water that downstream countries need to survive.

discovery.text: 200+ river treaties exist worldwide. Most use fixed allocations, but droughts make fixed shares unworkable.

twist.text: Game theory suggests benefit-sharing: instead of dividing water, divide the economic gains from cooperation.

climax.text: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project sells water to South Africa and shares revenue. Both nations gain more than alone.

punchline.text: Don't split the water—split the gains.

quiz.question: What does benefit-sharing mean in water conflicts?
options: Countries divide economic gains from cooperation

hook.text: A farmer clears rainforest for cattle. The world loses carbon storage. The farmer feeds their family. Who's wrong?

buildup.text: Deforestation is a global dilemma: local economic gains cause global environmental losses that nobody pays for.

discovery.text: REDD+ pays developing nations to keep forests standing. Norway paid Brazil $1.2 billion to cut Amazon deforestation.

twist.text: Monitoring is hard: satellite data shows deforestation shifted to smaller, harder-to-detect clearings. The game adapted.

climax.text: Mechanism design insight: align local incentives with global goals. Pay communities per hectare of standing forest.

punchline.text: Make keeping the tree worth more than cutting it.

quiz.question: How does REDD+ address deforestation?

hook.text: In 1985, scientists found a hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica. By 1987, the world agreed to fix it. It worked.

buildup.text: CFCs destroyed ozone, raising skin cancer risk globally. Every country benefited from CFCs but suffered from ozone loss.

discovery.text: The Montreal Protocol banned CFCs. It succeeded because substitutes existed, costs were low, and benefits were clear.

twist.text: Sanctions enforced participation: countries that didn't sign couldn't trade CFC products. Defection was costly.

climax.text: The ozone layer is healing. Full recovery is expected by 2060. It's the most successful environmental treaty in history.

punchline.text: When the solution is cheap, cooperation follows.

quiz.question: Why did the Montreal Protocol succeed where climate treaties struggle?
options: Cheap substitutes and trade sanctions made cooperation easy

hook.text: Every AI lab wants to pause and build safe AI. But if they slow down, competitors will race ahead. Nobody pauses.

buildup.text: The AI safety dilemma: safety costs time, and time means falling behind. Each lab faces pressure to ship fast.

discovery.text: This mirrors nuclear arms races: both sides prefer mutual slowing, but neither can risk unilateral restraint.

twist.text: Open letters calling for AI pauses failed—signatories kept developing. Without enforcement, pledges are cheap talk.

climax.text: Game theory suggests binding agreements with verification: AI safety standards that all labs must meet before deploying.

punchline.text: Everyone wants to slow down. Nobody wants to go first.

quiz.question: Why do AI safety pledges fail?
options: Without enforcement, slowing down loses competitive advantage

hook.text: Every app wants your attention. You want to spend less time on your phone. But each app is designed to be addictive.

buildup.text: Attention is a commons: platforms compete for the same finite resource—your time. Each designs for maximum engagement.

discovery.text: No single platform benefits from being less addictive. Users would just spend that freed time on a competitor's app.

twist.text: This is a race to the bottom: platforms that don't manipulate lose users to those that do. Ethics costs market share.

climax.text: Regulation is the mechanism: the EU's Digital Services Act limits dark patterns. Changing the game changes the behavior.

punchline.text: Your attention is the commons being overgrazed.

quiz.question: Why can't individual platforms choose to be less addictive?
options: Users would switch to more addictive competitors

hook.text: A company finds a software flaw. Report it and everyone benefits. Exploit it and only they profit. Most stockpile.

buildup.text: Nations and hackers hoard zero-day exploits. Disclosing fixes software; hoarding preserves attack advantage.

discovery.text: The NSA stockpiled exploits. When one leaked, WannaCry ransomware hit 200,000 computers in 150 countries.

twist.text: Bug bounty programs pay up to $250,000 for critical flaws. Money shifts incentives toward disclosure.

climax.text: Coordinated disclosure agreements try to solve this: report the bug, give the company 90 days, then go public.

punchline.text: One hoarded secret can compromise millions.

quiz.question: Why do nations stockpile software vulnerabilities?
options: Exploits provide attack advantage over fixing the flaw

hook.text: You accept cookies for convenience. Every user does. Now companies have everyone's data and nobody has privacy.

buildup.text: Data privacy is a social dilemma: each person shares data for small benefits, but mass sharing harms everyone.

discovery.text: Your data alone is harmless. Combined with millions, it enables surveillance, manipulation, and discrimination at scale.

twist.text: Individual opt-outs don't work: if your friends share data, companies infer yours anyway from patterns and connections.

climax.text: GDPR uses collective enforcement: companies face massive fines for misuse. Individual action can't solve group problems.

punchline.text: Privacy is a public good, not a personal choice.

quiz.question: Why can't individuals solve the data privacy dilemma alone?
options: Others' sharing reveals your data through patterns

hook.text: A doctor prescribes antibiotics 'just in case.' The patient feels better. But bacteria evolve resistance for everyone.

buildup.text: Each antibiotic use brings tiny resistance risk. Multiply by billions of prescriptions and resistance grows inevitable.

discovery.text: By 2050, drug-resistant infections could kill 10 million per year—more than cancer. Antibiotics are a depleting commons.

twist.text: New antibiotics aren't profitable: they're used sparingly and briefly. Drug companies have no incentive to develop them.

climax.text: Pull incentives offer prizes for new antibiotics regardless of sales. Mechanism design can fix the broken market.

punchline.text: Every unnecessary pill steals from the future.

quiz.question: Why is antibiotic resistance a social dilemma?
options: Individual use depletes a shared resource for everyone

hook.text: Should governments mandate carbon cuts or let companies volunteer? Volunteers rarely show up to dilemma games.

buildup.text: Voluntary approaches let defectors profit: companies that don't cut emissions save money over those who do.

discovery.text: Regulations change the game: if everyone must cut equally, no one gains competitive advantage from polluting.

twist.text: But regulations can be captured: industries lobby to weaken rules. The fox designs the henhouse.

climax.text: The best solutions combine both: set mandatory floors with voluntary bonuses. Punish defection, reward leadership.

punchline.text: Voluntarism asks nice. Regulation makes sure.

quiz.question: Why does voluntary action often fail in social dilemmas?
options: People don't know about the problem
Defectors gain competitive advantage over cooperators

hook.text: If nobody owns the field, nobody cares for it. Give someone ownership and they'll maintain it. Problem solved?

buildup.text: Privatization solves some dilemmas: owners internalize costs and benefits. A rancher won't overgraze their own land.

discovery.text: Coase's theorem: if property rights are clear and trading is free, private bargaining achieves efficient outcomes.

twist.text: But some commons can't be privatized: oceans, air, biodiversity, and knowledge don't respect property boundaries.

climax.text: Privatization works for rivalrous, excludable goods. For everything else, we need collective solutions.

punchline.text: Ownership works—but only for things you can fence.

quiz.question: When does privatization fail to solve social dilemmas?
options: When resources can't be divided or excluded

hook.text: Austria has 99% organ donor rates. Germany has 12%. The only difference: Austria's form is opt-out; Germany's is opt-in.

buildup.text: Nudges change behavior without bans or mandates: redesign the choice architecture so the default is the social optimum.

discovery.text: Thaler and Sunstein showed small design tweaks shift massive populations: default enrollment doubled 401(k) sign-ups.

twist.text: Critics call it 'libertarian paternalism'—you're free to choose, but the deck is stacked toward the 'right' answer.

climax.text: Richard Thaler won the 2017 Nobel Prize. Over 200 'nudge units' now exist in governments around the world.

punchline.text: Change the default, change the world.

quiz.question: Why are nudges effective in social dilemmas?
options: They change defaults so cooperation requires less effort

hook.text: Solar panels were too expensive until enough people bought them. Economies of scale kicked in and prices plummeted 89%.

buildup.text: Threshold models show that cooperation can suddenly become self-sustaining once enough people participate.

discovery.text: Granovetter's model: each person has a threshold. Join a riot if enough others do. One threshold triggers the next.

twist.text: Small pushes at the right moment cause massive shifts. Getting from 20% to 25% adoption can tip the entire system.

climax.text: EVs hit this tipping point: enough early buyers created charging infrastructure that attracted mainstream buyers.

punchline.text: Get enough people over the line, and the rest follow.

quiz.question: What is a tipping point in social dilemmas?
options: When enough cooperators make cooperation self-sustaining

hook.text: Before a prisoner's dilemma, both players promise to cooperate. Then 60% defect anyway. Promises are cheap.

buildup.text: Cheap talk is communication that costs nothing and can't be enforced. Game theory predicts it should be ignored.

discovery.text: But experiments show pre-game communication increases cooperation by 40%. Even cheap talk changes behavior somewhat.

twist.text: Face-to-face talk works better than written messages. Seeing someone lie is harder—empathy and guilt activate.

climax.text: Diplomacy relies on cheap talk: summits, hotlines, and treaties build expectations without binding enforcement.

punchline.text: Talk is cheap, but silence is cheaper.

quiz.question: Why does cheap talk sometimes increase cooperation?
options: It creates expectations and activates social pressure

hook.text: Every dollar spent on weapons makes your rival spend a dollar too. Neither side is safer, but both are poorer.

buildup.text: Arms races are social dilemmas: arming feels safer, but mutual arming leaves everyone equally threatened and poorer.

discovery.text: The US and USSR spent $10 trillion on nuclear weapons during the Cold War. Neither gained lasting strategic advantage.

twist.text: Arms control treaties are cooperation mechanisms: both sides limit weapons, with inspections to prevent cheating.

climax.text: The START treaties cut nuclear arsenals by 80%. Verification—not trust—made cooperation possible between adversaries.

punchline.text: Security isn't about more weapons—it's about fewer for everyone.

quiz.question: Why are arms races social dilemmas?
options: Both sides prefer mutual disarmament but fear unilateral restraint

hook.text: If you pay taxes and your neighbor cheats, you fund the roads they drive on for free. You're the sucker.

buildup.text: Tax compliance is a social dilemma: everyone benefits from public services, but each person saves by not paying.

discovery.text: Studies show compliance is contagious: if you believe others pay, you pay. If you believe others cheat, you cheat too.

twist.text: The IRS found that telling people '9 out of 10 neighbors pay on time' increased compliance more than threatening audits.

climax.text: Design solutions: withholding at source, third-party reporting, and digital trails reduce tax evasion by design.

punchline.text: Good systems collect taxes; great ones make cheating pointless.

quiz.question: What increases tax compliance most?
options: Believing most others pay their taxes

hook.text: If 95% are vaccinated, the virus can't spread. So why get jabbed? Let others take the tiny risk and free ride.

buildup.text: Herd immunity is a public good: once enough people vaccinate, even the unvaccinated are protected. Free riding tempts.

discovery.text: As vaccine rates drop, herd immunity breaks: measles outbreaks returned in communities with vaccination rates below 90%.

twist.text: Social media amplified vaccine fears. A few vocal anti-vaxxers shifted equilibrium from high to low vaccination.

climax.text: Mandates work: states requiring school vaccination keep rates above 95%. Structure beats persuasion in dilemmas.

punchline.text: Herd immunity fails when too many free ride.

quiz.question: Why is vaccination a social dilemma?
options: Individuals can free ride on herd immunity

hook.text: A new road opens and traffic gets worse. How? More people drive because road looks faster, until it's not anymore.

buildup.text: Braess's paradox: adding capacity to a network can worsen everyone's outcome when users choose routes selfishly.

discovery.text: Each driver takes the fastest-looking route, but everyone doing this overloads it. The Nash equilibrium is gridlock.

twist.text: Seoul demolished a highway in 2003 and traffic improved. Removing roads can fix congestion by eliminating shortcuts.

climax.text: Congestion charges, real-time navigation, and bus lanes redesign the game so individual choices align with the group.

punchline.text: More roads can mean more traffic.

quiz.question: What is Braess's paradox?
options: Adding road capacity can worsen congestion

hook.text: A rumor spreads: the bank is failing. Everyone rushes to withdraw. The bank was fine—until the rush killed it.

buildup.text: Bank runs are self-fulfilling: if you believe others will withdraw, withdrawing is rational. Belief creates reality.

discovery.text: Diamond and Dybvig modeled this: banks work because not everyone withdraws at once. A panic breaks this equilibrium.

twist.text: SVB collapsed in 2023 after Twitter-fueled panic. $42 billion withdrawn in hours—a social media bank run.

climax.text: Deposit insurance solves the dilemma: if your money is guaranteed, there's no reason to run. The FDIC prevents panics.

punchline.text: The run itself creates the crisis it fears.

quiz.question: How does deposit insurance prevent bank runs?
options: It removes the incentive to withdraw first

hook.text: Satellite launches leave debris. Each piece risks collision. Collisions create more debris. The sky fills with junk.

buildup.text: Kessler syndrome: enough debris triggers a cascade of collisions, making entire orbits unusable for decades.

discovery.text: Low Earth orbit is a commons: no one owns it, launching is cheap, and cleanup costs are shared by everyone.

twist.text: SpaceX launched 5,000+ Starlink satellites. Each company racing to fill orbits makes the debris problem worse for all.

climax.text: Solutions: orbital use fees, debris removal bonds, and international liability rules. Mechanism design for space.

punchline.text: The sky is a commons we haven't learned to share.

quiz.question: Why is space debris a social dilemma?
options: Launches benefit individuals but debris harms everyone

hook.text: If one country allows genetic enhancement, parents elsewhere face pressure: enhance your kids or they fall behind.

buildup.text: Genetic enhancement creates an arms race: nobody wants it, but nobody can afford to opt out if others start.

discovery.text: Like doping in sports, the equilibrium shifts: if cheating is common, clean competition becomes impossible.

twist.text: Unlike sports doping, genetic changes are permanent and heritable. The stakes are generations, not one race.

climax.text: International coordination is the only solution: a ban that all countries enforce, like bioweapons treaties.

punchline.text: When enhancement starts, opting out isn't an option.

quiz.question: Why is genetic enhancement an arms race?
options: If others enhance, opting out means falling behind

hook.text: We burn fossil fuels for comfort today. Future generations pay the price. They can't negotiate, vote, or protest.

buildup.text: Intergenerational dilemmas pit present selves against future people who have no voice and no power.

discovery.text: Economists use 'discount rates' to weigh future costs. A small rate change shifts trillions in optimal climate spending.

twist.text: Nicholas Stern argued for low discount rates: future lives matter as much as ours. Others disagreed. The debate rages.

climax.text: Constitutional protections for future generations now exist in Wales, Hungary, and several other countries.

punchline.text: The hardest dilemma: the other player isn't born yet.

quiz.question: What makes intergenerational dilemmas uniquely difficult?
options: Future generations can't participate in decisions

hook.text: A perfect deepfake of a president declaring war goes viral. By the time it's debunked, markets have crashed.

buildup.text: Cheap deepfakes create a trust dilemma: if any video might be fake, all video evidence loses credibility.

discovery.text: This enables the 'liar's dividend': real scandals get dismissed as deepfakes. Truth loses its power.

twist.text: Detection tools exist but face an arms race: each detection advance spurs better fakes. Defense always trails offense.

climax.text: Cryptographic provenance—signing video at capture—could create verifiable chains of truth. A new trust institution.

punchline.text: When nothing looks fake, everything does.

quiz.question: What is the 'liar's dividend' from deepfakes?
options: Real evidence gets dismissed as potentially fake

hook.text: We banned CFCs, controlled smallpox, and reduced nuclear arsenals. Social dilemmas can be solved. But not all of them.

buildup.text: Success needs: visible harm, cheap solutions, few players, and enforceable agreements. Climate change has none.

discovery.text: Evolution shows cooperation rising: cells cooperated into organisms, organisms into societies. The trend is upward.

twist.text: Each solution creates new dilemmas. International law solved wars but created free-riding alliances. Progress spirals.

climax.text: Game theory doesn't eliminate dilemmas—it reveals their structure so we can design better institutions around them.

punchline.text: We can't end dilemmas, but we can get better at them.

quiz.question: What determines whether a social dilemma can be solved?
options: Visible harm, cheap solutions, few players, and enforcement
